items.name: Irritant damage, not an allergy
body: The NHS splits contact dermatitis
in two: an irritant directly damages
the outer layer of skin, an allergen
makes the immune system respond
Contact dermatitis is most commonly
caused by irritants, and the
allergic form is the less common one
DermNet notes that occupational hand
dermatitis is caused by irritants in
80 percent of cases

items.name: Patch testing answers a different question
body: Patch testing tapes small amounts of
known allergens to the back and
reads them over several days
It answers the allergy question,
but it does not diagnose irritant
damage
If your skin only reacts after long
pool sessions and calms down over
the following week, that is a
barrier problem

items.name: The smell is chloramine, not chlorine
body: CDC explains that chloramines form
when chlorine combines with
nitrogen-containing material that
swimmers bring in: sweat, dirt,
pee and poop
Chloramines are what irritate skin,
eyes and airways, and most health
departments cap them at 0.4 ppm
CDC recommends pH 7.0 to 7.8 and
free chlorine of at least 1 ppm
in pools

items.name: Rinse going in, rinse coming out
body: CDC's reasoning for the pre-swim
rinse: even a quick one removes much
of the body waste that forms
chloramines in the first place
So rinsing protects the water, and
the water then irritates you less
NHS prevention advice is to rinse
skin that has met an irritant with
warm water as soon as possible -
at the lunch break too, not just
at closing time

items.name: Swap the gel, moisturise while damp
body: The NHS suggests emollient soap
substitutes rather than regular bar
or liquid soaps, which dry the
skin out
Then gently dry and apply the
emollient while the skin is still
moist, in a large amount, smoothed
in the direction hair grows
For very dry skin, two to four times
a day; ointments hold moisture best

items.name: What hydrocortisone can and cannot do
body: The NHS instruction is blunt: do not
use hydrocortisone on your skin for
more than 7 days unless a pharmacist
or doctor tells you to
Apply a thin layer once or twice a
day; a fingertip unit covers an area
twice the size of your palm
If you also use an emollient, apply
that first and wait around 30 minutes

items.name: When to stop self-treating
body: Hydrocortisone is the wrong choice
on broken skin, cold sores,
chickenpox, shingles or a bacterial
skin infection
Get seen if the rash covers a large
area, blisters are spreading, you
have a fever, or it has not settled
after about two weeks
After stopping a steroid cream,
intense redness, burning or peeling
is a reason to call NHS 111

headline: The pool did not do this on its own.
The gap between getting out and
getting moisturised did
Rinse, pat dry, apply while damp -
that sequence is the whole
intervention
tip: Put a tube of plain emollient in the swim bag next to the towel, so the decision is already made when you are cold and tired
If your skin keeps reacting after every swim, ask a pharmacist or GP about testing rather than cycling through products
